newsitem.title: UK: Euro petchem margins seen pressured for rest year.
newsitem.headline: Euro petchem margins seen pressured for rest year.

text.p: European petrochemical margins are likely to be under sustained pressure for the rest of 1997, producers and traders said on Thursday.

The pressure is coming from the lowest spot prices for ethylene - the main bulk petrochemical - since this time last year, by full cracker utilization across Europe and by firm prices for dollar-denominated feedstocks, principally naphtha and Liquified Petroleum Gas (LPG).

"Ethylene prices are already below $500 a tonne in the Mediterranean and are heading that way in the north," said a Benelux trader. "Further downward price pressure through the rest of the year is what I'm afraid of."
Ethylene spot prices were last seen below $500 CIF North West Europe in the third quarter 1996 before rising to close to $700 a tonne in late first quarter 1997.
Prices plateaued at those levels before slipping to the mid $600s by first half July, but these slumped to current levels on plentiful supply.
"With naphtha and the dollar stronger, we're going to see a little bit of a squeeze on petchem margins, although they will remain comfortable," a leading U.S.-based producer said.
Although current naphtha physical prices in the low to mid-$190s a tonne are some way from the $220-$230 highs experienced last winter, they have risen by around $25 from early July lows.
Dramatic dollar gains over the past year have meant naphtha prices in marks have recently been around DM360 a tonne, just DM30 short of the post Gulf war highs seen last winter.
While petrochemical feedstocks are priced in dollars, downstream commodities like plastics are sold within Europe in local currencies, dominated by the mark.
Few currency analysts have dared to predict a significant short term reversal in the dollar's strength, and the likely direction of crude and products prices is far from clear.

Petrochemical players said that virtually all west European petrochemical crackers, which produce ethylene and propylene for downstream plastics production and benzene for gasoline blending, are currently operating at or close to full capacity.

The second quarter round of cracker turnarounds and an ensuing period of unexpected outages are now seen to be over, with last weekend's earlier-than-expected restart of a problem-hit Dow Chemical Co cracker in Terneuzen in the Netherlands seen as the last of a series of recent hitches.
Barring a fresh spate of incidents, traders and producers agree that the normal summer slowdown in downstream demand will conspire with good ethylene availability to pressurize spot prices.

They say the fourth quarter, which normally signals a surge in demand and prices, will this year be marked by oversupply pressures as large-scale new European polypropylene and polyethylene plants come onstream.
Although another round of fourth quarter cracker turnarounds are scheduled, much less capacity will be taken down than in the second quarter.
Traders also said the market had already allowed for the fourth quarter shutdowns, the impact of which will therefore be very limited.
